intro.title: Quantum jobs are not only for people with a PhD
intro.text: A PhD is a degree you earn after college. Scientists with PhDs do important work, but a quantum facility also needs people who run equipment, write software, protect data, keep buildings working, ship parts and manage projects. Here is what the evidence says.

stats.label: of the quantum job postings the Chicago Quantum Exchange studied for 2023 asked for a bachelor's degree or less. Companies and nonprofits were higher, at about two in three postings.
of the jobs analysts expect in Illinois, Wisconsin and Indiana by 2035 (as many as 191,000) are predicted to be open to people with a bachelor's degree, an associate degree or technical training.

intro.parkTitle: What the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park says it will need
intro.parkText: The park is being built on the old South Works steel site. Its FAQ page lists these kinds of jobs:
intro.honestText: A job that does not require a PhD is not always an entry-level job. The Chicago Quantum Exchange found that many postings asked for experience in a related field, such as computer science or engineering. That is why every career below lists jobs you can do today that build toward it.

quiz.title: Which part of quantum might fit you?
quiz.intro: Five questions, about one minute. There are no wrong answers, and we do not ask who you are. Your answers are never saved or sent anywhere.

questions.question: Which sounds like the best way to spend a Saturday?

options.text: Taking something apart to see how it works, then putting it back together
Building a game, app or website on a computer
Cracking a secret code or solving a mystery
Fixing or wiring something in the garage or around the house
Planning an event or a project with friends

questions.question: On a big group project, which job would you grab first?

options.text: The builder, who makes the model with their hands
The coder, who writes the program that makes it run
The defender, who finds weak spots before anyone else does
The fixer, who keeps everything working when something breaks
The organizer, who keeps everyone on schedule and supplies coming

questions.question: Which problem would you most like to help solve?

options.text: Making machines colder, faster or more precise
Teaching computers to do something brand new
Keeping people's private information safe online
Keeping a big building's power, cooling and water running
Helping a neighborhood get fair access to new jobs and training

questions.question: How do you like to work?

options.text: Careful, hands-on work with small parts, in a lab or workshop
Moving around a big site, solving problems on the spot
At a computer, with quiet time to focus on a hard problem
Spotting small details that other people miss
Talking with a team about plans and deadlines

questions.question: Which of these would you be proudest to say you did?

options.text: Helped build a machine that does something nobody has done before
Wrote a program that thousands of people use
Stopped an attack that would have exposed people's private information
Kept an important building running every day without a hiccup
Helped bring new jobs and training to my neighborhood

results.intro: This is a starting point, not a test. You can change your mind any time, and many people work in more than one of these areas over a career.
results.tieNote: These came out even, so we are showing both.

interestAreas.label: Hardware
interestAreas.blurb: Building, testing and running the machines themselves.
interestAreas.matchText: You like understanding how things work and building them with care. Quantum machines are made of lasers, tiny electronics and very sensitive parts, and people who can assemble, test and run them are in demand. Several of these jobs start with a technician role, not a PhD.

interestAreas.label: Software
interestAreas.blurb: Writing the code that controls and uses quantum computers.
interestAreas.matchText: You like turning ideas into working programs. Every quantum computer needs software to control it, plus tools that let other people use it. If you already enjoy coding, this is a direct path, and the Learn pages on this site are a good place to start.

interestAreas.label: Cybersecurity
interestAreas.blurb: Protecting data and systems from attacks.
interestAreas.matchText: You like puzzles and noticing what others miss. Future quantum computers could break some of the locks that protect data today, so security teams are already planning upgrades. Defending information is a skill that works in almost every industry.

interestAreas.label: Trades & facilities
interestAreas.blurb: Building, wiring and running the spaces that quantum machines live in.
interestAreas.matchText: You like practical work and seeing the result of what you do. A quantum park needs people to wire buildings, run cooling equipment and keep everything working every day. Many of these jobs can be reached through apprenticeships, where you learn on the job.

interestAreas.label: Business & policy
interestAreas.blurb: Planning, supplying, organizing and speaking up for the people involved.
interestAreas.matchText: You like making plans happen and bringing people together. Labs and parks need people to manage projects, move parts, and talk with city and state leaders. These roles help make sure a big project actually serves the neighborhood around it.

educationLevels.label: High school diploma
educationLevels.blurb: A high school diploma or GED. Some jobs and apprenticeships start here.

educationLevels.label: Certificate
educationLevels.blurb: A focused training program that teaches one set of job skills.

educationLevels.label: Associate degree
educationLevels.blurb: A two-year college degree, such as one from a community college.

educationLevels.label: Graduate degree
educationLevels.blurb: A master's degree or PhD, earned after a bachelor's degree.

cardLabels.relatedJobs: Jobs that build toward it today
cardLabels.relatedJobsIntro: These jobs are not in quantum, but they build the same skills:

careers.summary: Helps scientists and engineers run experiments by setting up equipment, collecting data and keeping the lab working.
dayToDay: Set up and check the equipment for an experiment.
Collect data on a computer and write down what you see.
Notice when something is not working and help fix it.
Keep tools and supplies organized and safe.

educationPaths.note: The Chicago Quantum Exchange found technician postings, such as an R&D Technician job, that did not list a degree, though many non-PhD jobs still ask for related experience.
A research report that interviewed quantum employers lists lab technician as a job an associate degree can lead to.
The same report lists a bachelor's degree too, which keeps more doors open later.

localResources.name: Saturday Morning Quantum (Fermilab)
localResources.note: A free Saturday lecture series open to all high school students, with no science prerequisite. Talks cover special topics and Fermilab career opportunities.

localResources.name: Quantum Quickstart (Chicago Quantum Exchange)
localResources.note: A one-week quantum summer program for Illinois high school students, offered at no cost to selected participants. Preference goes to students in the city of Chicago.

localResources.name: Chicago Quantum Exchange Talent Portal
localResources.note: A free tool that lists job and internship openings at quantum employers, so you can see what real postings ask for.

careers.summary: Puts together delicate quantum equipment, then tests that every piece works the way it should.
dayToDay: Assemble parts such as lenses, lasers and electronics.
Clean and inspect delicate optics (the glass parts that guide light).
Run tests and measurements, then record the results.
Keep the paperwork for parts and finished equipment in order.

educationPaths.note: The Chicago Quantum Exchange lists an Assembly Integration Test Technician posting that did not name a degree, but many non-PhD jobs still ask for related experience.
Chicago State University lists a Semiconductor Technology and Manufacturing certificate, a field close to this hands-on work.
A report that profiled this kind of job lists an associate or bachelor's degree in subjects such as math, optics or physics.
Researchers who interviewed employers list a bachelor's degree for photonics assembly technicians (photonics means working with light).

localResources.name: Chicago State University CQuEST
localResources.note: Chicago State's quantum education center. It lists a Semiconductor Technology and Manufacturing certificate and is open to career-changers as well as new students.

localResources.name: Chicago Quantum Exchange Talent Portal
localResources.note: A free tool that lists job and internship openings at quantum employers.

careers.summary: Runs a quantum computer day to day, scheduling jobs on it and making sure it keeps working.
dayToDay: Start up, watch and look after the quantum system.
Schedule the programs that people send to the machine.
Spot problems early and fix them or pass them to the right team.
Write down what happened so the team knows.

educationPaths.note: A report that profiled this job lists a bachelor's degree in engineering or physics and says operators are trained on the job.

relatedJobs: Data center or IT help-desk technician

localResources.name: Quick Quantum: For High Schoolers (Chicago Quantum Exchange)

careers.summary: Designs, builds and improves the machines that scientists use to test quantum ideas.
dayToDay: Build and adjust lasers, lenses and electronics for an experiment.
Work out why a measurement looks wrong.
Plan the next test with your team.
Explain results clearly to teammates.

educationPaths.note: The Chicago Quantum Exchange found that engineering postings mostly asked for only a bachelor's degree.
Researchers who interviewed employers list a master's degree for research engineers, and many scientist jobs ask for a PhD.

careers.summary: Writes programs that run on quantum computers and on the regular computers that control them.
dayToDay: Write and test code for quantum and regular computers.
Turn a scientist's rough code into tools other people can use.
Find and fix bugs (mistakes in code).
Talk with scientists to turn their ideas into programs.

educationPaths.note: Chicago State University lists a Quantum Information Science & Engineering certificate for undergraduates.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says software developers typically need a bachelor's degree, and a quantum software profile lists the same.
The quantum software profile also lists master's and PhD degrees, and some employers prefer a master's.

localResources.note: A YouTube series for high schoolers that introduces quantum information science and engineering.

careers.summary: Builds the regular software around a quantum computer, such as the websites and tools people use to send it work.
dayToDay: Build tools that let people send jobs to a quantum computer over the internet.
Connect programs to each other through APIs (ways for programs to talk).
Build and run the systems that test and monitor the machines.
Fix problems and improve the code as people use it.

educationPaths.note: City Colleges of Chicago lists Software Development among its tech programs, and its Moonshot program connects people to paid tech apprenticeships.
A profile of this job lists a bachelor's degree, and says strong coding skills matter most and internships help.
The same profile also lists master's and PhD degrees.

careers.summary: Protects an organization's computers and networks by watching for attacks and fixing weak spots.
dayToDay: Watch security alerts and decide which ones are real.
Find weak spots in systems before attackers do.
Help coworkers set up safer passwords and tools.
Write short reports on what happened and what to change.

educationPaths.note: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says some analysts enter with a high school diploma plus industry training and certifications.
The same source says many employers prefer to hire people who hold an information security certification.
City Colleges of Chicago lists Cybersecurity among the tech programs in its Moonshot program.
A bachelor's degree in a computer science field is the typical starting point, and some jobs ask for related work experience.

localResources.name: City Colleges of Chicago Moonshot
localResources.note: Connects people to paid tech apprenticeships and an affordable associate degree in tech. Listed programs include Cybersecurity and Networking & Systems.

localResources.note: Says IBM FutureNow Chicago is preparing to hire Chicago roles in cybersecurity, AI and quantum.

careers.summary: Helps organizations switch to new kinds of encryption (a way of scrambling data) that quantum computers could not break.
dayToDay: Find where your organization uses encryption today.
Plan and test the move to the new quantum-safe standards from NIST, the U.S. standards agency.
Update systems step by step, because the full switch takes time.
Explain to coworkers why the change matters.

educationPaths.note: Many employers prefer security certifications for analysts, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Information security analysts typically hold a bachelor's degree in a computer science field.

careers.caution: Job titles for this work vary, and it is often part of a wider security job. NIST finished its first quantum-safe encryption standards in August 2024 and encourages system administrators to begin switching as soon as possible.

careers.summary: Runs and looks after the equipment that keeps quantum machines extremely cold.
dayToDay: Watch gauges, screens and alarms on the cooling equipment.
Do routine checks and keep a log of what you find.
Fix small problems and report big ones.
Follow safety rules around very cold materials.
skills: Staying calm when an alarm goes off

educationPaths.note: Similar plant jobs, such as stationary engineers, require a high school diploma and are learned through on-the-job training or apprenticeships.
For those similar jobs, vocational classes can help workers move up as the work gets more complex.
College classes can help too, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

careers.summary: Installs and repairs the wiring, lighting and power that a lab or factory runs on.
dayToDay: Install and repair wiring, lighting and power systems.
Follow building plans and electrical safety codes.
Test equipment to find where a problem is.
Work alongside other trades on a building site.

careers.summary: Helps build and maintain labs, including cleanrooms, which are super-clean spaces where dust cannot ruin delicate parts.
dayToDay: Check that equipment is placed and installed correctly.
Keep mechanical connections in good shape.
Do electrical and plumbing work in a lab.

careers.summary: Makes sure the right parts and supplies arrive on time, and that finished equipment ships out with the right paperwork.
dayToDay: Check that deliveries match what was ordered.
Track what is in stock and what is running low.
Pack and ship equipment with the right paperwork.
